clue.text: Sweet treat dunked in senega tea, unusually

indicators.note: Dunking pushes something down below the surface of what surrounds it, so the letters wanted are submerged in the words that follow.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters, starting in the middle of the first word and finishing in the third

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' looks like an anagram signal and is really just more hiding place: the letters need no shuffling, and a comma is no barrier to a concealed run.
explanation.definitionFit: A gateau is a rich iced cake, the French word English keeps for the fancy end of the trolley rather than everyday baking.

clue.text: Following write-up, I am able to take on one person skilled at thought

indicators.note: To follow is to walk behind, so everything named afterwards is written after the first piece rather than before it.
A firm that takes someone on brings them inside it, so the piece named next is absorbed rather than added at the end.

blocks.note: a log is the written-up record of what happened
the clue's own pronoun, taken as a letter
'I can' is 'I am able' — and this is the word that opens up
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a job application, which is why the break after 'write-up' is invisible: 'I am able' stops being a boast and becomes three separate scraps of spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A logician works professionally at reasoning, so the definition is thought as a discipline with rules rather than anyone who happens to think hard.

clue.text: Those in charge crushing a surreal rebellion

indicators.note: To crush something is to squash it out of existence, so the little word it lands on never reaches the answer.
A rebellion overthrows the established order, and the letters left behind end up in a new order too.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, before the deletion
the article is squashed out, taking one A with it

explanation.walkthrough: On the surface a coup is being put down; underneath, the rebellion is what does the damage, and it only starts once a single letter has been crushed.
explanation.definitionFit: Rulers are the people holding power over a country, which is what being in charge amounts to; the thing in a pencil case is a different sense.

clue.text: Leader of group to sign and approve, please

indicators.note: A leader walks at the front of the party, so what is handed over is the letter standing at the front of the word.

blocks.note: the first letter of Group
to ratify a treaty is to sign it formally into force

explanation.walkthrough: Two verbs sit at either end of this clue and the quiet one is the definition: 'please' as something you do to a person, not the word you add to a request.
explanation.definitionFit: To gratify someone is to give them pleasure or satisfaction, which is 'please' in its verb sense rather than the polite formula.

clue.text: Leaves off career to retrain, and succeeds in the end

indicators.note: What comes at a word's finish is its final letter, and every word in this run hands over whichever letter it stops at.

blocks.note: ofF — last letter
careeR — last letter
tO — last letter
retraiN — last letter
anD — last letter
succeedS — last letter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface tells a complete story about a mid-life change of job, so the instruction sitting at the end of it reads as the happy ending rather than as directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Fronds are the long divided leaves of a fern or a palm, so the definition is the botanical sense — a particular kind of leaf, not foliage in general.

clue.text: Sunk in snow-drifts – is getting out what might cause difficulty?

definitions.note: The definition is a description rather than a noun: 'what might cause difficulty' names a set of things, so it stands in for a plural.

indicators.note: Getting out is leaving, so the little word named just before it walks away instead of joining the mix.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, before the deletion
these two letters are the ones that leave

explanation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of a full stop. Everything before it is a car buried in a drift; everything after it is a two-letter word climbing out before the shake-up.
explanation.definitionFit: The unknowns in a plan are the things nobody can put a value on yet, and it is exactly those that make a job hard to finish.

clue.text: Island getting upset over EU operation

blocks.note: the Isle of Man, the crossword's default island
anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: A bare 'island' is worth trying as MAN before anything else — the Isle of Man, Iona and Elba are the three the setters reach for.
explanation.definitionFit: A manoeuvre is a planned movement of troops or vehicles, which is 'operation' in the sense of an exercise carried out rather than surgery.

clue.text: Bird in bamboo across river

indicators.note: A thing laid across another lies over it from one side to the other, so the letter named next is covered rather than followed.

blocks.note: bamboo is a giant cane
R is the mapmaker's abbreviation for river

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird in bamboo' sounds like a hiding place and isn't: 'in' is only joining the definition to the wordplay, and the real instruction is the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A crane is a tall long-legged wading bird; the lifting machine took its name from the bird's outstretched neck, not the other way round.

clue.text: I’m welcomed by chaps following soldiers in big groups

indicators.note: To be welcomed by someone is to be taken into their house, so these letters end up inside the word that does the welcoming.
Following a body of men means walking along behind them, so this piece is written after them rather than in front.

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, the two letters a clue's soldiers nearly always want
gents is the everyday word for chaps, and it is what splits open
the clue's own two words, taken as two letters

explanation.walkthrough: RE for Royal Engineers is worth learning by heart: soldiers, sappers and engineers all point at the same pair of letters, and one of them turns up most weeks.
explanation.definitionFit: A regiment is a permanent army unit made up of several battalions, so 'big groups' is the plain sense — large bodies of people organised together.

clue.text: Senseless, not sharp in the head, unbalanced

indicators.note: A plain negative is enough to take something away: what comes after it is what the longer word has to do without.
The head of a word is its front, so all that is meant by it is the single letter the word begins with.

blocks.note: someone unbalanced is out of their mind
the letter at the head of Sharp — this is the one that goes

explanation.walkthrough: Three comma-separated insults, and each is doing a different job: the first defines, the middle pair name a letter to lose, and the last supplies the word to lose it from.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means empty of meaning — an inane remark carries nothing at all, which is what calling it senseless says.

clue.text: Really big game to play

indicators.note: Play is the slack in a rope or a hinge, and letters with that much give in them will not stay where they were put.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playground slang, which is fair but never the first sense you meet: the word is really the scientific prefix for a million, let loose as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Mega is the prefix meaning a million, borrowed as slang: a mega party is an enormous one, so it stands in for 'really big'.

clue.text: Suited to perform services

indicators.note: A piece is performed in whatever arrangement the players work it up into — a loose signal, but the only word here asking for anything to be done.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: When the first word of a three-word clue has exactly as many letters as the enumeration asks for, try shuffling it before you try anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: Duties are the tasks a post obliges you to carry out, and services covers the same ground: work owed rather than a favour freely given.

clue.text: Worries, as wife’s picked up tools

indicators.note: A car that picks you up takes you inside it, so the letter collected here sits within the short word beside it, not after it.

blocks.note: to fret is to worry away at something
the clue's own word, taken as two letters and then prised apart
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s here is 'has', pure grammar, and belongs to the DIY scene on the surface rather than to the letters — not every 's in a clue is an S.
explanation.definitionFit: A fretsaw is the fine-bladed saw used for cutting curves in thin wood, so 'tools' defines by category rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Give up wearing a ring?

blocks.note: the clue's own article, taken as a letter
a wedding band is a ring
the clothes you are wearing are the ones you have on

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is the phrase 'a band on', which is all that wearing a ring amounts to — and the question mark is there because the whole sentence can be read that way.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon something is to give it up for good and walk away from it, rather than merely handing it over to someone else.

clue.text: Facilitated purchase of very poor chianti?

blocks.note: someone broke has run out of money altogether
chianti is a Tuscan wine, and the question mark admits it is only one example of the colour

explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to three words and the wordplay to two, and the join is invisible because 'purchase of very poor chianti' reads as one miserable shopping trip.
explanation.definitionFit: To broker a deal is to arrange it between buyer and seller, so the past tense answers 'facilitated purchase of' — the middleman's verb.

clue.text: State how you might answer phone within two rings

indicators.note: Within means inside the boundary of a thing, so the greeting goes between the pair named next rather than beside them.

blocks.note: a ring drawn on the page is an O, and the clue asks for a pair of them
the two-letter greeting you say when you pick up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Within two rings' is telephone etiquette on the surface and an instruction underneath — the same three words doing both jobs without changing a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ohio is a midwestern American state, so 'State' defines by example: one of fifty, chosen because its spelling happens to suit the wordplay.

clue.text: Most stupid to try bucking trend first

indicators.note: A bucking horse throws its rider over its own head, and the word it is attached to lands the other way round.
First means at the front of the answer, so the piece just turned round goes ahead of the other one.

blocks.note: a passing trend is a fad, written backwards
to try something out is to test it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bucking trend' is one idea on the surface — going against the fashion — and two separate instructions underneath, which is why the seam is so hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Daft is the friendly British word for silly, so its superlative covers 'most stupid' without the sting the plainer word carries.

clue.text: Having a depiction that’s only skin-deep?

definitions.text: Having a depiction that’s only skin-deep?

indicators.note: This is the word that turns a thing into an adjective about its owner — a man with money is moneyed, a man with a beard bearded.

blocks.note: a picture that goes no further than the layer of skin it is inked into
the ending English adds to say someone owns one: moneyed, bearded, talented

explanation.walkthrough: There is no second half to hunt for: the sentence defines the answer and builds it at the same time, which is what an all-in-one clue does.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tattooed carries a design inked into the skin, so 'only skin-deep' is meant literally here rather than as the usual dismissal of something superficial.

clue.text: Angrily berated one making an argument

indicators.note: Anger throws things about without caring where they land, so the word beside it comes apart and is put back differently.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: Berating someone angrily is precisely what the answer is not meant to do: a debate is an argument conducted with rules and a chairperson.
explanation.definitionFit: A debater argues a case formally, for or against a motion, so the definition is 'argument' in the reasoned sense rather than a row.

clue.text: Teaching medic to withhold oxygen in first sign of emergency

indicators.note: To withhold something is to keep it back, so the letter named after it never reaches the answer.
The first sign of anything is whatever shows at the very start, which here is one opening letter.

blocks.note: the everyday word for a medic, before it is made to give something up
O is oxygen's symbol on the periodic table — this is what is held back
the clue's own word, taken as two letters
the first letter of Emergency

explanation.walkthrough: A first-aid scene on the surface, and it is the second O the medic loses. Watch 'in': here it is two letters of the answer, not the link word it usually is.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctrine is a body of teaching held and handed on by a church or a party — teaching as the thing taught, not the act of doing it.

clue.text: School leaver?

blocks.note: the phrase everybody knows: a sixteen-year-old who has finished their education and is looking for a job
the question mark is the whole warning — take 'leaver' literally, as somebody walking out during the day rather than at the end of the years

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here to take apart: no indicator, no fodder, no letters to move. When a two-word clue offers none of those, it is one phrase with two readings and you want the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A truant leaves school without permission, so the answer takes 'leaver' at its word, while the phrase as a whole normally means someone who has finished school.

clue.text: Someone like me puts tester to use

indicators.note: Putting something to use means finding a fresh job for it, and letters given a fresh job turn up in a fresh order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Me' is the person who wrote the clue — a standing crossword joke — and 'tester' describes what they are doing to you while you read it.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter is the compiler who writes the puzzle, so 'someone like me' is that person pointing at themselves: a convention worth learning early.

clue.text: Ms Hathaway is on the way up, Ms Miller

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so anything travelling upwards is read from the bottom of the column back to the top.

blocks.note: the first name of the actor who starred in The Devil Wears Prada
the clue's own word, taken as two letters

explanation.walkthrough: Two actors in one short clue: one supplies letters and the other is the definition, and the join between them is the little word 'is' doing no grammatical work at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Ms Miller is the actor Sienna Miller, so this is a definition by example — her first name doubles as the earthy red-brown pigment.

clue.text: Slips on slips?

blocks.note: the everyday word for small mistakes, the kind that get through proofreading
in publishing these are printed on a loose leaf of paper tipped into the front of the book

explanation.walkthrough: The same word twice, in two senses — the setter's whole joke, and the question mark is the only sign that a pun rather than a repetition is intended.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are an author's slips in the sense of mistakes, and they reach the reader on a slip of paper bound into the book: both senses at once.

clue.text: ‘Kentish Spirit’ is thin, watery liquid

blocks.note: Kent sits in the south-eastern corner of England
rum is the sailor's spirit, distilled from sugar cane

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks dress the first two words up as the name of a pub or a boat, which is exactly why they do not look like a compass point and a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Serum is the pale watery part of blood that is left once the clot is taken out, which the definition describes exactly.

clue.text: Of course, they are spectators!

blocks.note: the throwaway agreement — naturally, obviously — which is how the sentence asks to be read
the second reading takes the two words before it literally: these are the people of the course, out at the rails watching

explanation.walkthrough: Two words carry the whole joke: 'of course' is an idiom on the surface and a possessive underneath, and the exclamation mark is the setter's nudge that something is up.
explanation.definitionFit: The crowd at a meeting are spectators of a course in the most literal sense the phrase allows, which is what the pun turns on.

clue.text: Some soave in small vessels

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it and not the whole, so what is wanted is a stretch of letters cut out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters, running across the ends of three words in a row

explanation.walkthrough: An Italian white and a tasting note make a smooth surface, and the definition waiting at the end of it turns out to be anatomical rather than nautical.
explanation.definitionFit: Veins are the vessels that carry blood back to the heart, so 'vessels' is the anatomical sense of the word rather than ships or jars.

clue.text: Puts a new spin on horse-based air conditioning?

blocks.note: the strap a rider steers with, and it is based on the horse
the slatted openings air conditioning blows through

explanation.walkthrough: The surface invents an absurd product and the question mark apologises for it, which is enough to hide the fact that the first three words are a plain definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinvent something is to make it over into a new form, which is what putting a new spin on a thing means: presenting it afresh.
